html:
A Roman aqueduct in Segovia, central Spain, built around the end of the 1st century CE. It carried water about 17 km from mountain springs to the town's fountains, baths and houses, and it was still in use in the 20th century.

Its famous part is the arcade that crosses the valley in the middle of town: 167 arches of granite blocks, set without mortar, rising to about 28 metres at the highest point. The exact date is uncertain; many scholars place it under Domitian or Trajan.

In 1072, during an attack on the town from the Muslim kingdom of Toledo, part of it was destroyed. The Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, had it rebuilt in the 1480s. It went on carrying water until the 1970s.

It is one of the best preserved Roman aqueduct bridges, with the Pont du Gard, and appears on Segovia's coat of arms. It is a lasting mark of Roman Hispania, one of the most Romanised parts of the Roman Empire.
